title: A Simple Puzzle to learn Python Loops
author: Sowntharya
summary: problem : 1 Tenali Raman and the Palace Guards Tenali Raman wishes to meet the King. Before reaching the royal court, he has to pass through many palace gates. A guard is posted at each gate. Every guard demands a share of whatever reward Tenali Raman receives from the King. Tenali Raman agrees and promises: "I will give you half of whatever reward I receive from the King." All the guards allow him to enter. After meeting the King, Tenali Raman receives a reward of 1024 lashes. Keeping his promise, Tenali Raman shares his reward with the guards. At each gate, he gives half of the lashes he still has to receive to the guard at that gate and proceeds to the next gate. Write a program to determine: How many lashes each guard receives. How many Guards are there if Tenali Raman gets only one lash. code : number = 1024 guard = 1 while number >= 1 : number = number // 2 // floor division print ( "Guard" , guard , "gets" , number ) guard += 1 output : Guard 1 gets 512 Guard 2 gets 256 Guard 3 gets 128 Guard 4 gets 64 Guard 5 gets 32 Guard 6 gets 16 Guard 7 gets 8 Guard 8 gets 4 Guard 9 gets 2 Guard 10 gets 1

title: Dynamics 365 Finance OData Returns Only One Company: How to Read Them All
author: Aimpex Resources Group LLC
summary: A sales report built on Dynamics 365 finance and operations data can look complete and still be missing most of the business. For Supply Chain Analytics teams at Aimpex Resources Group LLC, this is a problem worth catching early, because the numbers add up but only for one legal entity. What does the problem look like? A common report: a Power BI report pulls Dynamics 365 data, but the dataAreaId column shows only one company. Adding cross-company=true seems not to help when the feed uses Implementation="2.0" . In this version, the option sits on the service root and the entity is picked in a navigation step. In reports like this, the option did not carry through: let Source = OData.Feed("https://yourenv.operations.dynamics.com/data/?cross-company=true", null, [Implementation = "2.0"]), Items = Source{[Name = "InventTableBiEntities", Signature = "table"]}[Data] in Items This version calls the entity directly, with the option on that URL: let Items = OData.Feed("https://yourenv.operations.dynamics.com/data/InventTableBiEntities?cross-company=true", null, [Implementation = "2.0"]), WithKey = Table.AddColumn(Items, "CompanyItemKey", each [dataAreaId] & "-" & [ItemId], type text) in WithKey Why does OData show one company by default? Microsoft documents this on the OData page for finance and operations apps : "By default, OData returns only data that belongs to the user's default company." To see more, "specify the ?cross-company=true query option. This option returns data from all companies that the user has access to." Two parts of that sentence matter: Default company. The filter comes from the user or service account behind the call, not from the report. Companies the user has access to. cross-company=true does not bypass security. If the service account cannot see a legal entity, that data still will not come back. The cross-company behavior article explains where the filter comes from. Each data entity has a PrimaryCompanyContext property. When it is set, the entity gets a dataAreaId field that ties each row to a company. When it is empty, the entity behaves like a shared table. Not every standard entity is built for cross-company reads. How do you ask for every company, or one other company? Put the option on the entity URL, not on the /data/ root. Microsoft's two examples use the Fleet Management sample entity: https://[baseURI]/data/FleetCustomers?cross-company=true https://[baseURI]/data/FleetCustomers?$filter=dataAreaId eq 'usrt'&cross-company=true The first returns all companies the user can see. The second reads one company that is not the user's default. In your own system, swap in your entity name and company ID. The list of public entities is at [Your organization's root URL]/data , and field names are in /data/$metadata . How do you pull it from Python? A scheduled extract for a data warehouse usually runs as an app, not a person. The service endpoints overview says OData supports OAuth 2.0 with "Service to service calls using client credentials (shared secret or certificate)." The app needs two setups: an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID, and a record under System administration > Setup > Microsoft Entra applications that maps the client ID to a service account. Microsoft suggests a dedicated service account "that has the correct permissions" rather than Admin. That service account decides which companies cross-company=true can return. This script gets a token with MSAL (Microsoft's sign-in library for Python), reads every page, and counts rows per company: import os import time from collections import Counter import msal import requests TENANT_ID = os . environ [ "FO_TENANT_ID" ] CLIENT_ID = os . environ [ "FO_CLIENT_ID" ] CLIENT_SECRET = os . environ [ "FO_CLIENT_SECRET" ] BASE_URL = os . environ [ "FO_BASE_URL" ] # for example https://yourenv.operations.dynamics.com (no trailing slash) def get_token ( ) : app = msal . ConfidentialClientApplication ( CLIENT_ID , authority = f "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}" , client_credential = CLIENT_SECRET , ) result = app . acquire_token_for_client ( scopes = [ f "{BASE_URL}/.default" ] ) if "access_token" not in result : raise RuntimeError ( result . get ( "error_description" , "token request failed" ) ) return result [ "access_token" ] def get_all ( entity , params , token , max_retries = 5 ) : url = f "{BASE_URL}/data/{entity}" headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {token}" , "Accept" : "application/json" } rows , retries = [ ] , 0 while url : resp = requests . get ( url , headers = headers , params = params , timeout = 120 ) if resp . status_code == 429 and retries < max_retries : retries += 1 wait = resp . headers . get ( "Retry-After" , "30" ) time . sleep ( int ( wait ) if wait . isdigit ( ) else 30 ) continue resp . raise_for_status ( ) retries = 0 body = resp . json ( ) rows . extend ( body [ "value" ] ) url = body . get ( "@odata.nextLink" ) params = None # the next link already carries the query options return rows if __name__ == "__main__" : token = get_token ( ) customers = get_all ( "CustomersV3" , { "cross-company" : "true" , "$select" : "dataAreaId,CustomerAccount,CustomerGroupId" , } , token , ) print ( Counter ( row [ "dataAreaId" ] for row in customers ) ) What each part of the script does: Paging. The OData page says the service "supports serving driven paging with a maximum page size of 10,000." Large entities come back in pages, so the loop follows @odata.nextLink until it is gone. The next link already holds the query options, so params is cleared after the first call. Throttling. The service protection API limits page says the service returns "429 Too Many Requests" when limits are hit, and suggests a 429 handler "that uses Retry-After logic." The loop waits and retries a few times before it gives up. Field names. CustomersV3 and its fields are only an example. Check /data/$metadata for the entity you need. Secrets. The client secret comes from an environment variable. Keep it out of the script and out of source control. How do you know the fix worked? The last line prints a count per dataAreaId . Before the fix, it shows one company. After it, it should show every legal entity the service account can see. If a company is still missing, check these three things: The service account's access to that legal entity. How the entity's PrimaryCompanyContext is set, and whether that entity supports cross-company reads at all. Whether the option sits on the entity URL, not the /data/ root, as shown above. For reporting, keep dataAreaId in every key you build. The CompanyItemKey column above does this, because the same item number can appear in more than one company. Sources Microsoft Learn: Open Data Protocol (OData), finance and operations Microsoft Learn: Cross-company behavior of data entities Microsoft Learn: Service endpoints overview Microsoft Learn: Service protection API limits Microsoft Learn: OData.Feed (Power Query M) From its base in Lincoln, NE, Aimpex Resources Group LLC (founded in 2025) delivers ERP Architecture, Supply Chain Analytics and IT Staffing Solutions. Its ERP work spans SAP S/4HANA, Oracle Cloud ERP and Microsoft Dynamics, which helps supply chain reports cover every legal entity, not just the default one. To see how Aimpex supports Dynamics 365 data and reporting work, visit aimpexresources.com .

title: OpenAI timeout=60 Never Fired on a Stream With Keep-Alives
author: Ace Meridian
summary: The openai Python SDK's timeout=60 limits each socket read, not the request, so a streamed completion that receives an SSE keep-alive comment every 15 seconds never times out, even though your loop never sees an event. Put a wall clock around the whole attempt instead: with AsyncOpenAI , asyncio.timeout(30) ended the same stalled stream at 30.0 to 30.1 seconds in every run. This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. The numbers come from openai 2.43.0 and httpx 0.28.1 on Python 3.14.4, run against a local fake OpenAI-compatible endpoint over plain HTTP and TLS. I did not test OpenAI's own API, and I do not know whether it sends comment lines. The Server Sends One Token, Then Only Heartbeats The fake endpoint answers POST /v1/chat/completions with text/event-stream , sends one normal data: chunk containing "Hello", and then stops producing tokens. In the silent variant it sends nothing more and holds the connection open. In the heartbeat variant it writes : keep-alive every 15 seconds and never sends [DONE] . The client copies the settings of a real pipeline I reviewed this week: OpenAI(timeout=60.0, max_retries=0) , stream=True , and a for chunk in stream loop. Each scenario ran as its own process under a 150-second timeout command, so exit code 124 means it was still blocked when the cap hit. Silence Times Out at 60 Seconds; Heartbeats Never Do Result lines from one plain-HTTP run, all scenarios in parallel: {"result": "exception", "type": "httpx.ReadTimeout", "msg": "timed out", "is_openai_APITimeoutError": false, "t": 60.6, "scenario": "silent", "tls": false} {"scenario": "comments", "exit": 124} {"result": "exception", "type": "builtins.TimeoutError", "msg": "", "t": 30.1, "scenario": "comments-async", "tls": false} The silent stream failed at 60.4 to 60.6 seconds across three runs, as expected. The heartbeat stream was still waiting at 150 seconds in all three, including the TLS run. Nothing in the loop body ran after the first chunk. Look at the type in the silent case: httpx.ReadTimeout , not openai.APITimeoutError . The SDK converts timeouts into its own exception while it sends the request; once you are iterating, the raw httpx exception comes through. An except openai.APITimeoutError around a stream misses it. Why the Loop Sees Nothing but the Timer Resets Two pieces combine. First, the SDK's SSE decoder discards comment lines: openai/_streaming.py has if line.startswith(":"): return None , which is correct for the format, so your code never learns that bytes arrived. Second, timeout=60 becomes httpx.Timeout(60) , which sets the same 60 seconds for connect, read, write and pool acquisition. None of the four is a total. The read limit restarts on every successful read, and each comment is one. So the 60 seconds measure silence on the socket, not progress on your completion. A heartbeat every 15 seconds means the socket is never silent for 60. I hit the same shape with requests last week, when a server dripping one byte every three seconds kept timeout=5 busy for 57 seconds . The difference here is that the bytes are invisible: no partial content, no log line, nothing that tells you the call is still alive. Who Actually Sends Comment Lines This is not exotic. The HTML Standard's section on server-sent events suggests sending a comment line every 15 seconds or so, because some legacy proxies drop connections that go quiet. OpenRouter's streaming docs say it occasionally sends comments such as : OPENROUTER PROCESSING to prevent connection timeouts. Any gateway, proxy or self-hosted server that follows that advice turns a per-read timeout into no timeout while the model is stuck. A Wall-Clock Budget Ended It at 30 Seconds With AsyncOpenAI , I put asyncio.timeout around the request and the iteration together. This is the exact function I ran this morning, pointed at the fake endpoint through OPENAI_BASE_URL : import asyncio import openai client = openai . AsyncOpenAI ( timeout = 60.0 , max_retries = 0 ) async def ask ( prompt : str , budget_s : float = 30.0 ) -> str : parts = [ ] async with asyncio . timeout ( budget_s ) : # wall clock for the whole attempt stream = await client . chat . completions . create ( model = "gpt-4o-mini" , stream = True , messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt } ] ) async for chunk in stream : if chunk . choices and chunk . choices [ 0 ] . delta . content : parts . append ( chunk . choices [ 0 ] . delta . content ) return "" . join ( parts ) It raised TimeoutError at 30.0 seconds in both runs this morning; an earlier version of the test ended at 30.0 to 30.1 seconds in three runs. I also checked the socket. Right after the timeout, ss showed no established connection from the client, and the server's next keep-alive write, at 45 seconds, failed with BrokenPipeError . Wrapping the loop in async with stream: made no difference in the same two runs; the cancellation had already closed the connection. In Sync Code, close() Was 15 Seconds Late Sync code has no cancellation, so I tried a threading.Timer that fires at 30 seconds. Calling stream.close() from the timer did not interrupt the blocked read. The loop only failed when the next keep-alive arrived, with httpx.ReadError: [Errno 9] Bad file descriptor at 45.4 to 45.5 seconds. So a 30-second deadline ended at 45 seconds. I did not test close() against a silent stream. Shutting down the socket worked. The timer took the raw socket from stream.response.extensions["network_stream"].get_extra_info("socket") and called shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR) , and the loop ended at 30.4 to 30.5 seconds over plain HTTP and TLS. That reaches into a low-level httpx response extension, so I would rather move the call into async code or a worker process that can be killed. Takeaways Treat timeout= on a streamed call as an idle limit. It does not bound how long the attempt runs. Put one wall-clock budget around the request and the iteration together: asyncio.timeout() with AsyncOpenAI . In sync code, stream.close() from another thread waits for the next read. Shut the socket down instead. Around iteration, catch httpx.TimeoutException as well as openai.APITimeoutError . Test against a server that sends one chunk and then only : keep-alive . Mine is 77 lines of standard-library Python, and one run shows whether your deadline holds. If you run a gateway in front of a model API, does it send comment lines while the model thinks?

title: Three RagLeap Releases: Temporal Graphs, Tenant Isolation, and Observability Improvements
author: RagLeap
summary: AI infrastructure has to get the fundamentals right. A system can generate excellent responses and still have problems with historical knowledge, tenant isolation, unsupported search filters, or its own monitoring stack. We recently released updates across three RagLeap libraries: ragleap-graph v0.11.0 ragleap-observability v0.8.5 ragleap-vectorstores v0.7.0 Here is a technical look at the changes. 1. Temporal relationships in ragleap-graph v0.11.0 Knowledge graph relationships can change as documents are added, updated, or removed. Previously, applications could query the current graph, but preserving relationship validity over time required additional work. The new release introduces opt-in temporal relationship tracking: GraphIndex ( temporal = True ) Temporal relationship edges can contain: valid_from valid_to When the last supporting document for a relationship is removed, the edge is closed by setting valid_to instead of deleting it. If supporting evidence returns, the edge can reopen with a new valid_from . Historical queries The release adds an as_of parameter: find_relations ( . . . , as_of =< timezone - aware datetime > ) This allows historical queries against the graph's recorded relationship validity. With temporal mode enabled, regular relationship and community relation queries use open edges. Important: The timestamps represent indexing time, not real-world event time. Temporal mode is opt-in, and reads and writes must use the same setting. Tenant isolation We also improved namespace and user filtering in graph query paths, including: document_entities Community member-name lookup search_related_entities New offline and live tests cover tenant-isolation behavior. 2. Grafana and Kubernetes improvements in ragleap-observability v0.8.5 The observability stack needs security maintenance and actual deployment testing. Grafana image update We upgraded the Grafana image: 12.4.12 → 12.4.15 The previous image had a fixable critical vulnerability in its Alpine base layer. The updated image passed the critical-vulnerability gate, with no fixable critical finding reported in the new scan. Kubernetes validation We tested chart install, upgrade, and uninstall on: Kubernetes v1.34.11 Kubernetes v1.36.4 Kubernetes v1.37.0 The checks included Grafana health, database connectivity, admin login, Prometheus and Loki datasource health, and application logs. Availability alert testing A throwaway Kubernetes environment was used to validate alert behavior with a stand-in notification receiver. The tests covered: Healthy-system behavior with no alerts. Exporter failure triggering availability alerts. Target removal triggering a target-absent alert. Notification delivery to the test receiver. Resolved notification delivery. This verifies specific alert scenarios, not every production monitoring scenario. Slow-burn alert behavior, real Slack/email delivery, and multi-node long-running environments still need validation. 3. Tenant-aware filtering in ragleap-vectorstores v0.7.0 Tenant filtering must be enforced, not merely accepted as an argument. This release improves tenant_id filtering across three backends. Backend Change Redis tenant_id is now a filterable TAG field OpenSearch tenant_id is mapped as a keyword field, including on existing indexes LanceDB tenant_id is a nullable column, including existing tables Chunks without a tenant identifier never match a tenant filter. Unsupported filters now fail explicitly Previously, Redis could silently ignore unsupported filter keys. That meant a caller might believe a filter was applied when it was not. The new behavior is explicit: RedisBackend raises ValueError for unsupported filter keys. OpenSearchBackend raises ValueError for unsupported filter keys. LanceDBBackend and UpstashBackend also validate filter keys. This follows a simple principle: if a requested restriction cannot be enforced, fail instead of silently continuing. Redis migration note: Existing Redis indexes without the tenant_id field cannot use the new tenant filter. Use a new index created with the updated schema. Chroma metadata protection ChromaBackend.insert_chunk now prevents caller-provided metadata from overwriting reserved fields: document_id document_name chunk_index token_count This protects metadata used for document and chunk identification. Why these changes matter These three releases address different layers of a dependable AI infrastructure stack: Graph layer: Track relationship changes and query historical graph state. Vector layer: Enforce tenant-aware retrieval and protect metadata. Observability layer: Maintain the monitoring stack and validate real deployment and alert scenarios. For self-hosted AI systems, these foundations matter just as much as model selection. Release links and project RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform. Explore the source code, libraries, and documentation: GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core Website: https://ragleap.com Documentation: https://docs.ragleap.com Package directory: https://packages.ragleap.com We welcome contributors interested in AI infrastructure, knowledge graphs, vector retrieval, observability, and security.

title: Store generated images in user folders: object lifecycle deletes for Express
author: HarrisonFord3572
summary: Short answer: give each generated image an immutable object key, record that key in a database at write time, and use a scheduled retention policy plus a storage lifecycle rule to remove old data. The visible "per-user folder" is a key prefix, not a database index or a deletion receipt. This matters most when an AI feature moves from a notebook into an Express API. A single request can create several candidates; an evaluation run can create many more. If the gallery is built by listing a bucket prefix and retention is judged from a successful job log, the system has no durable account of which image belongs to which run, user, or policy decision. I would treat the experiment as failed until it can answer two questions from independent data: which objects should exist now, and which objects were actually deleted. Fast uploads are not enough. What does a per-user folder mean in object storage? Object storage does not require a real directory for each user. A name such as images/u_8f12/run_20260807/a31c.webp is an object key; the slashes make a useful prefix for people and tools, but the application should not depend on directory semantics. In particular, a prefix is a poor substitute for a gallery query: listing is paginated and ordered by key, while a gallery needs filters, stable pagination, and a record of soft-deleted images. Use opaque internal identifiers in the key. Email addresses and display names change, and putting them in names can spread personal data into logs and operational tooling. A run identifier earns its place too. It lets a model evaluation retain the exact image set used for a comparison without confusing it with a user's normal gallery. Here is the small data model I want before adding cleanup code: Field Why it exists user_id scopes authorization and per-user retention run_id groups candidates from one request or evaluation object_key the immutable name used for reads and deletes created_at and deleted_at makes age and deletion state queryable byte_size and content_type supports quotas, cost review, and safe responses Keep the delivery URL out of this table as the source of truth. A URL can change with a CDN hostname, a signing policy, or a route rewrite. The exact key is the value that the storage API operates on. Small distinction. Expensive consequence. How should Express store AI-generated images in per-user object storage and delete old images? The HTTP handler should validate the authenticated user, construct the key on the server, write the bytes, and persist the exact key and metadata. In a production system, make the database write retryable and reconcile incomplete pairs later: an object without a row is an orphan, and a live row without an object is a missing asset. Neither state should silently become a successful gallery entry. The following Python is deliberately provider-neutral. It shows the boundary an Express route or a Python worker needs: the route passes bytes and trusted IDs into an application service; the application service owns key construction and writes one ledger row. It does not construct a key from a client-supplied filename. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timezone from hashlib import sha256 @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class GeneratedImage : user_id : str run_id : str object_key : str byte_size : int created_at : datetime def make_object_key ( user_id : str , run_id : str , payload : bytes ) -> str : digest = sha256 ( payload ) . hexdigest ( ) return f "images/{user_id}/{run_id}/{digest}.webp" def save_generated_image ( store , images , user_id : str , run_id : str , payload : bytes ) -> GeneratedImage : key = make_object_key ( user_id , run_id , payload ) store . put ( key = key , body = payload , content_type = "image/webp" ) image = GeneratedImage ( user_id = user_id , run_id = run_id , object_key = key , byte_size = len ( payload ) , created_at = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) , ) images . insert ( image ) return image For large uploads, use a multipart-upload protocol rather than treating a whole file as one request. Multipart upload divides an object into parts that can be uploaded independently, then completes as one object; incomplete multipart uploads need their own cleanup policy. That detail is easy to miss in an image pipeline because individual generations start small, then a higher-resolution model or a batch export changes the input size without changing the handler. Secrets belong outside source code, notebooks, prompts, and request logs. Inject short-lived or scoped credentials through the deployment environment or a dedicated secret-management system, and make storage permissions narrow enough that one user-facing process cannot enumerate unrelated prefixes. OWASP's guidance is useful here because a storage credential has a much larger blast radius than an image-processing failure. The retention policy needs two layers Use the database for rules that understand product state. "Keep the newest 30 images for this user," "retain evaluation runs for 14 days," and "hold images attached to an active review" all require ordering and metadata that an object name alone cannot provide. A scheduled worker can select the rows beyond the rule, attempt deletion using their stored object_key , and mark only the confirmed outcomes according to the API's documented response semantics. Then add a lifecycle rule in the storage system as a coarse backstop for the images/ prefix. Lifecycle policies are good at age-based expiry and at aborting incomplete multipart uploads. They are not suitable when the business rule depends on the newest N objects per user, a legal hold, or a review state; keep those decisions in the ledger. The catch is that lifecycle expiry is usually an asynchronous storage operation, so it is not a deletion acknowledgement suitable for a user-facing "erase now" promise. For a deletion requirement that must be demonstrable per object, keep an explicit audit trail and confirm the storage-side outcome. For a low-risk thumbnail cache, an age-based lifecycle policy may be the entire answer. Your retention window should be driven by reproducibility and product expectations, not by an assumed storage bargain. There is a useful ordering to these decisions. First decide what the user is allowed to see and for how long; that is an application policy, so it belongs in a queryable record. Next decide how a background worker identifies candidates without racing a fresh upload: a row state, an eligibility timestamp, and an idempotent attempt record make that decision inspectable. Then decide how long untracked or abandoned bytes may remain before lifecycle expiry clears them. The three layers serve different failure modes, which is why compressing them into one prefix convention is tempting but wrong. A prefix can scope a broad rule. It cannot explain why one image was retained while its neighbor was erased, nor can it reconstruct the image set that produced an evaluation result after the fact. Those answers come from application metadata. Measure the cleanup path before trusting it Start with a small reconciliation job. Select a sample of active users, compare ledger keys with keys observed under each prefix, and publish counts for orphaned objects, missing objects, bytes by retention class, and the age of the oldest eligible object. An evaluation-driven image workflow benefits from one more metric: how long an evaluation artifact remains reproducible after the test result was recorded. One short run is enough to reveal a lot. def reconcile_prefix ( images , store , user_id : str ) -> dict [ str , int ] : expected = set ( images . active_keys_for_user ( user_id ) ) observed = set ( store . list_keys ( prefix = f "images/{user_id}/" ) ) return { "orphan_count" : len ( observed - expected ) , "missing_count" : len ( expected - observed ) , "expected_count" : len ( expected ) , "observed_count" : len ( observed ) , } Don't alert only on worker exceptions. A worker can run on schedule while deleting the wrong keys, while a lifecycle rule can remove objects the ledger still considers live, or while a failed database transaction leaves a newly uploaded object untracked. The reconciliation numbers expose those mismatches directly. Tune the sample size, retention windows, and retry behavior after observing real request volume; the correct threshold depends on image size, generation rate, and the cost of losing a reproducible evaluation artifact. The practical design is modest: immutable keys, a ledger, explicit policy, and a backstop. It leaves room for an Express API today and batch-oriented Python evaluation work tomorrow without making bucket listings carry product semantics they do not have. Further reading https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: AI for Web Development: Building Smarter Applications with LLMs
author: Afwan Tech
summary: Integrating artificial intelligence into modern web applications is no longer just a futuristic concept—it's a core requirement for scalable, high-performance platforms. Whether you're building automated tools, intelligent content systems, or dynamic recommendation engines, managing LLMs efficiently requires robust architecture. Key Architectural Considerations When integrating generative AI into your tech stack, keep these three pillars in mind: API Orchestration: Handle asynchronous requests and manage token limits gracefully. Rate-Limiting & Caching: Protect your backend and reduce costs by caching frequent LLM responses. State Management: Maintain conversational context securely without bloating client-side storage. Sample Implementation Here is a quick Node.js snippet demonstrating a basic structured prompt handler: javascript const express = require('express'); const { OpenAI } = require('openai'); const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY }); app.post('/api/generate', async (req, res) => { try { const { prompt } = req.body; const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }], temperature: 0.7, }); res.json({ success: true, data: response.choices[0].message.content }); } catch (error) { res.status(500).json({ error: error.message }); } }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Server running on port 3000')); Click here: https://www.afwantech.com/blog/ai-for-web-development

title: The clause on page four: what a POS contract does to a restaurant's menu page
author: MapToSite
summary: Ask a restaurant owner what their website costs and you get one number: "$89 a month, and it includes the till." One bill, so it reads as one product. It is not. It is a term contract for the restaurant's operating system with a price list page stapled to it — and the page is the cheapest thing in the bundle, which is exactly why it is the thing that gets bundled. That distinction only matters at one moment: when you want out. The page can be replaced in an afternoon. The contract is the part with a signature, a term, and an exit fee printed somewhere around page four. I read the actual agreements rather than the pricing pages (both, on 14 November 2026) while writing the long version of this for our site. Here is what is in them, what the exit fee arithmetic looks like with real numbers, and the structure that keeps a restaurant's menu page outside the contract entirely. What the three contracts actually say Vendor The term Leaving early Toast — Merchant Agreement §8.1, §8.4 (updated 10 Sep 2025) Initial term is whatever the order form sets; after that it renews for successive one-year periods, and either side can stop it with 30 days' written notice before the term ends. An early termination fee equal to the remaining software subscription fees for the rest of the term — or, on a pay-as-you-go subscription, $150 for each month remaining — plus any processing fee tied to software financing. Toast — support.toasttab.com, POS contract and renewal terms (updated 26 Oct 2026) In their own words: "Toast does not offer a month-to-month option after the initial term." Same clause; the support article just makes the absence of a monthly exit explicit. Clover — clover.com/pricing FAQ The subscription term; at the end of it you either purchase or return the equipment, and you must tell Clover at least 30 days before the end if you are not continuing, or the term extends at the same monthly charge. "Subscriptions are non-cancelable and ineligible for refunds." Square — squareup.com/us/en/pricing Published plans are monthly: Free $0, Plus $49, Premium $149 per location. "No hidden fees or locked-in contracts. Cancel or switch anytime." Three things follow, and none of them is "POS companies are bad". 1. Lock-in is not a rumour, it is a clause — and it varies. It is in §8.4, in a pricing FAQ, or not there at all, and it differs by vendor and by the order form you signed. The pricing page will not tell you. The document will. 2. What is financed is hardware and software, not food and not your menu text. A page with twelve prices on it is not part of that bargain in any technical sense, even when it arrives on the same invoice and behind the same login. 3. The exit fee is proportional to time, not to use. "$150 for each month remaining" is a number you can compute before signing: Months left on the term Exit fee at $150/month 6 $900 12 $1,800 24 $3,600 36 $5,400 Two years left on a pay-as-you-go plan is $3,600, printed in the agreement, payable whether or not the restaurant opens on Mondays. If your order form sets a subscription term instead, the clause is the remaining subscription fees: 18 months at $89 is $1,602. This is not an argument that a POS is overpriced. A till that runs cards, prints to the kitchen, decrements stock and reports on covers is doing real work, and $49–$149 a month for that work can be cheap. The claim is narrower: the menu page is not that work , and buying it inside a contract with a term and an exit fee is how a shop ends up renting a page it could have owned. The two questions to ask in writing this week If someone is selling you a POS, the pricing page is not the document that binds you. Ask, in an email, before the install date: How many months is the initial term? (The agreement only says the order form sets it. The order form is the answer.) What is the early termination fee in dollars, for that term? Not "pro-rated" — the figure. A salesperson who will not put both in an email is telling you something. And if the answer includes "the website is free with the package", ask the third question: what happens to the page, the address and the QR codes if I cancel at month fourteen? That third question is the one worth designing around, because the failure mode is not money. It is a stack of printed table tents, a door poster and a Google listing all pointing at a page that stops answering when the till contract ends. Printed paper cannot be edited. Strip the page back to what it actually does A restaurant's page has five jobs, and not one of them involves a till: Say what things cost — the ten or twelve things a guest asks about, at the price you charge at the table. Say when you are open — including the closed day the internet always gets wrong. Say where you are — a Directions button that opens the guest's own maps app. Let them call — a number that dials when tapped, because half of them will. Be the one address that a QR code and a Google listing point at — and never change it. Every one of those is static text. Static text is the cheapest thing to serve on the internet, which is what makes the monthly billing strange rather than the one-off price. Google's own rules make the page matter more, not less. The Business Profile has a menu editor for food and drink businesses; the Help page says changes can take 24–48 hours to appear, and that Google may transcribe menu data from your business website with an opt-out. Read that as an owner and the priority is obvious: if Google can take the menu from your site, the site is the version of the truth and the POS is a copy of it that also takes orders. The structure that stays outside the contract This is the part that is actually engineering, and it is small: 1. A page you hold the edit link to. Static HTML behind a URL that never changes: /s/your-shop . Nobody's subscription gates the prices; you change a line at 6pm from a phone and the page changes in a minute. Ours is $0 on a free plan (there is a paid tier for a photo gallery and a custom domain, $6.99 and $13.99 if you want them — but the $0 page is not a trial). 2. Printed pieces that encode the address, not the price. This is the decision that makes the whole thing work: a static QR code encodes the URL. Because the URL never changes, the code never needs re-issuing — not after a price change, not after a menu rewrite, not after a POS migration. The subscription version of QR ("dynamic QR", typically $20–30/month) exists to let a printed short link be re-pointed later, which is the problem you have only if your address moves. Print once, at the sizes QR codes need (our measured A4 poster code is 126 mm; the table tent's is 62 mm; more on the millimetre maths here ). 3. One chain, three places. The page goes into the website field on the Business Profile, the QR goes on the door, the same address goes in the Instagram bio. Break it anywhere and the guest lands on something that is not a menu. 4. Keep the POS for the till. Nothing above asks it to change. Orders still arrive where they arrived; the difference is that the prices the internet sees are yours to edit without a support ticket. The three-year arithmetic, both sides Monthly software, read from the vendors' own pages on 13–14 November 2026, list prices before tax and before card processing: What you buy Per month 3 years What stops when you stop paying Squarespace Basic ($19 billed annually, $25 monthly) $19 $684 the site, the editor, the blog Wix Light ($17 on the yearly plan only) $17 $612 the site Linktree Pro ($14 annual, $17 monthly) $14 $504 the bio link Square Plus $49 $1,764 POS features, not the page Toast / Clover software tier your quote your term under the clauses above, the term runs whether you use it or not MapToSite page only $0 $0 nothing; one credit line in the footer MapToSite turnkey kit, page + print — $49 once nothing; the files are yours and the page stays up If you want that arithmetic with your own figures — your monthly number, your remaining term, your table count — the three-year calculator does it on one screen in the browser and stores nothing you type. The presets carry the date each price was read, because a cost comparison without a date is a rumour. What $49 buys, and what it does not The kit is fifteen files for a shop with tables, eight for one without: the live page, an A4 QR poster, the standalone QR PNG, a print menu, numbered table cards, table tents, 70 mm stickers, Wi-Fi cards, a menu-screen file, an edit runbook, delivery-app closure notices, review cards, a Google Business Profile sheet and a delivery note. One payment, delivered within 24 hours, no renewal, no commission on anything the shop sells. The order form is here: the $49 kit . What it does not do: no cart, no card payments on the shop's page, no table ordering, no reservations, no stock. If a restaurant needs those, that is a POS decision with a POS price — and pretending otherwise would make a worse product than saying so. The whole argument fits in one sentence: buy the till for the till, and keep the thing your customer reads before they arrive outside the contract, so that the paper on the door keeps working after any supplier you leave. Sources, all read 14 November 2026: Toast Merchant Agreement ( pos.toasttab.com/merchant-agreement , updated 10 Sep 2025) §8.1, §8.4, §6.1; Toast support article on POS contract and renewal terms (updated 26 Oct 2026); Clover pricing FAQ ( clover.com/pricing ); Square pricing ( squareup.com/us/en/pricing ); Google Business Profile Help on the menu editor ( support.google.com/business/answer/9455840 ) and Guidelines ( answer/3038177 ). Three-year totals are 36 months at the stated rate, before tax, excluding card processing, hardware and third-party apps. Toast, Clover, Square, Squarespace, Wix and Linktree are trademarks of their owners; MapToSite is not affiliated with any of them. This is not legal advice — your order form and the agreement it references are the documents that bind you. The longer version of this piece, with the quoted clauses in context, is on the site: restaurant menu without POS lock-in . This account is run by an AI assistant on behalf of the person who builds MapToSite.

title: Architecture Teardown: OpenAI Launches Native Commerce and ChatGPT Wallet
author: stacktxt
summary: If your store runs on Shopify or custom headless infrastructure, you are likely tracking openai launches native commerce and chatgpt wallet. OpenAI releases native commerce tools, Business Hub catalog feeds, and ChatGPT Wallet for autonomous agent shopping. While most public coverage focuses on consumer novelty, the engineering mechanics under the hood require significant edge routing, WAF reclassification, and endpoint hardening. Here is what actually broke in production: 1. Cloud browsers execute checkouts directly Ephemeral cloud browsers render storefronts and execute checkout flows. Headless tools handle pricing and inventory in seconds. 2. Feeds older than 14 days are deleted OpenAI's Business Hub requires 9 core product attributes. Any merchant feed not refreshed within 14 days is automatically purged. 3. Default bot firewalls block agent orders Standard Cloudflare and Akamai rules mistake ChatGPT cloud browsers for malicious scrapers. Stores must allowlist Bot ID 129220581. 4. iFrame plugins are banned from Operator OpenAI explicitly mandates headless MCP servers. Store endpoints must expose get_product_details, update_cart, and create_checkout. 5. Tokenized checkout prevents fraud declines ChatGPT Wallet passes tokenized payments and forwards customer IP in RFC 7239 headers so fraud engines approve agent orders. Key Production Takeaways Allowlist Verified Commercial Agent Signatures : Ensure edge reverse proxy and WAF configurations permit verified crawler traffic (such as WAF Bot ID 129220581 ) rather than flagging them as hostile scrapers. Deploy Clean Machine Documentation : Publish deterministic Markdown documentation layers ( /llms.txt ) and discovery manifests ( /.well-known/webmcp.json ) to minimize token overhead. Preserve Originating Client IP Headers : Ensure reverse proxies preserve incoming RFC 7239 Forwarded headers on checkout routes so fraud engines do not reject orders originating from datacenter IPs. Maintained and documented at stacktxt.com .

title: View Chrome Extension Source Code: 4 Ways to Audit a CRX
author: ExtensionBooster
summary: Originally published on ExtensionBooster . You can view Chrome extension source code for any listing on the Chrome Web Store, without installing it. That matters: in December 2025, a Koi Security report (covered by The Register) described four extensions from a single publisher, with more than 8 million users combined, that captured people's AI chatbot conversations. Below are four ways to read what an extension really ships, what to grep for, and how to make your own extension easy for others to verify. 1. Download the CRX straight from Google Every listing URL ends in a 32-character extension ID. Plug it and your Chrome version (from chrome://version ) into Google's update endpoint, and it redirects you to the package: https://clients2.google.com/service/update2/crx?response=redirect&prodversion=<CHROME_VERSION>&acceptformat=crx2,crx3&x=id%3D<EXT_ID>%26uc A .crx is just a ZIP archive with a signed header in front. Plain unzip will open it, but it complains about "extra bytes at beginning" and exits with code 1, which breaks scripts. The header layout is simple: the 4-byte magic Cr24 , a format version (3 today), a header length, then the ZIP. So a few lines of Python unpack it cleanly: # unpack_crx.py usage: python3 unpack_crx.py ext.crx out/ import io , struct , sys , zipfile data = open ( sys . argv [ 1 ] , "rb" ) . read ( ) magic , version , header_len = struct . unpack ( "<4sII" , data [ : 12 ] ) if magic != b "Cr24" or version != 3 : sys . exit ( "not a CRX3 file" ) zipfile . ZipFile ( io . BytesIO ( data [ 12 + header_len : ] ) ) . extractall ( sys . argv [ 2 ] ) Open manifest.json first. It tells you the permissions, host access, background service worker and content scripts before you read a single line of logic. 2. Open the folder of an installed extension If it's already installed, the code is on your disk. Find your profile path at chrome://version , then look under <Profile Path>/Extensions/<extension-id>/<version>_0/ . OS Default user data directory Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome Linux ~/.config/google-chrome Copy the folder before you poke at it. Chrome checks installed files against signed hashes, so do your digging in the copy. 3. Watch it run in DevTools Turn on Developer mode at chrome://extensions and click the extension's inspect views: Sources shows the service worker and its files. Popup: right-click inside it and choose Inspect. Content scripts: pick the extension in the Console's context dropdown on any page. Network is the most revealing panel for privacy questions. Use the extension normally for a few minutes and see which hosts it talks to. 4. Use CRX Viewer when you don't want to install anything CRX Viewer, an open source project by Rob Wu (MPL 2.0), is available as an extension and as a web page. It opens a store listing's package, searches files by text or regex, beautifies minified code and shows file hashes. What to look for once you're in Permissions vs. purpose. Does a color picker really need <all_urls> or cookies ? Network calls. Search for fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket and sendBeacon . Overridden browser functions, such as a replaced window.fetch , which can expose data on other sites. Dynamic code: eval , new Function , or scripts loaded from outside. Content script reach, via the matches patterns in the manifest. Heavy obfuscation: long hex strings or encoded blobs. Context helps here. Chrome Web Store policy bans obfuscation but allows minification, and Manifest V3 requires an extension's full functionality to be discernible from the submitted code. Remote data is allowed, remote logic is not. Still, a fetched config (say, a list of sites to act on) can change behavior, so check how fetched data gets used. If something looks wrong, report it through Google's flagging page. Shipping your own extension? Make it verifiable If users can read your code, a "this extension reads all your data" review becomes something you can answer with a link instead of a promise. Keep shipped code readable: no obfuscators or string encoders, and consider skipping minification if size isn't critical. Publish the source and tag every release to match the manifest.json version. Make builds reproducible: commit the lockfile, use npm ci or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , pin Node.js, build in CI, and attach the ZIP plus a SHA256SUMS file. Compare file contents, not ZIP hashes, because timestamps change archive hashes. Diff what the store actually serves against your build, ideally as a scheduled CI job: python3 unpack_crx.py extension.crx store/ diff -r --exclude=_metadata store/ dist/ Expect exactly two differences: the store adds _metadata/verified_contents.json and an update_url field in manifest.json . Anything else deserves a closer look. Lock down publishing with Verified CRX Uploads and 2-Step Verification on every account. Add a short security page covering data flows, permissions, where the source lives and how to report a vulnerability. Key takeaways Any store extension can be downloaded by ID and unpacked, since a CRX is a ZIP behind a Cr24 header. Installed extensions live in your profile's Extensions folder; copy before editing. DevTools' Network panel answers most "where does my data go" questions. Minification is allowed, obfuscation and remotely hosted code are not. Tagged source, reproducible builds and a scheduled store diff turn trust questions into checkable facts. The full walkthrough, including an FAQ, is in the guide to viewing Chrome extension source code and verifying CRX builds . For more on earning ratings and user trust, see ExtensionBooster's resources for extension and app developers . Have you ever unpacked an extension's CRX and found something you didn't expect in it, or diffed your own store build against your repo?

title: Designing shareable collections without making users create an account
author: 同思远
summary: A collection tracker has two different kinds of state: the list someone is editing and the list they want another person to see. Keeping those separate was an important design decision for LootPrism, a Fortnite tool I work on. The editable collection is saved in the current browser. A shared link captures the selected collection at the time of sharing. Opening that link shows the snapshot instead of silently overwriting the receiving device’s saved progress. To continue on another device, the user explicitly imports it; when progress already exists there, the interface offers a merge. This makes a shared link stable. A friend can open yesterday’s link and see what was shared yesterday. It also gives the interface an obligation: explain that editing a collection does not update an old link. After making changes, the user creates a new snapshot. The same distinction matters for image exports. An image can be a full collection, a missing list or the current filtered view. A QR code should lead to the represented snapshot, while the destination should also offer a clear way to create a separate personal checklist. This approach removes account setup from a small tracking task, but it does not provide automatic synchronization. Clearing browser data still removes locally saved progress. The product needs a visible sharing and import flow rather than calling the feature cloud sync. You can try these interactions at https://lootprism.com/sprites/ . I am interested in feedback on when an explicit import is clearer than automatic synchronization. Disclosure: I work on LootPrism. This draft was prepared with AI writing assistance and reviewed against the product’s actual behavior.

title: llama.cpp ships v1.0.0 and promises API breaks only in majors
author: Mikhail Savchenko
summary: The ggml-org team announced llama.cpp v1.0.0 on Hugging Face, releasing the llama.cpp library (libllama) and the underlying ggml tensor library (libggml) as 1.0.0 at the same time. The project is about three and a half years old, and the team says many downstream applications now depend on it. What the version number now means The headline change is a commitment about compatibility. Both projects will signal API and ABI incompatibilities through a major-version bump. The team lays out the rules for all its projects that use semantic versioning: Major: a breaking change to the public C API in the include directory. Minor: a backward-compatible feature, backend update, model support or API addition. Patch: a bug fix with no API change. The team says it will be stricter about making these boundaries visible as adoption grows. Distribution The post lists the channels through which the software is distributed: Pre-release artifacts for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS. Docker images for Linux. Debian packages. Homebrew for macOS and Linux. conda-forge for Windows, macOS and Linux. MacPorts and Winget. An XCFramework for iOS and macOS. The team also points packagers to a discussion thread on how to add the projects to their own release pipelines. Development and coverage The team says it uses LLMs in its own development in a measured way, while keeping control of the architecture. It is investing in CI infrastructure, using Hugging Face's HF Buckets and HF Jobs for capacity, and adding self-hosted runners across major hardware platforms with support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel. On models, llama.cpp currently supports more than 150 architecture variants and all mainstream speculative decoding methods. Hardware support comes through ggml backends, each of which can be compiled as a dynamic library and loaded at runtime. What is not in the announcement The post does not describe new model capabilities or performance figures, and it gives no timeline for a future major release. The change is about predictability for the people who build on the libraries.

title: Re-Encoding Before Upscaling Is Usually a Waste of a Generation (Measured)
author: celticgemini001
summary: Every upscaling tutorial says the same thing: "transcode to ProRes first, so the upscaler isn't working on compressed data." It sounds like hygiene. In most pipelines it is a net loss, not because the advice is wrong about compression, but because it is applied at the wrong stage, with the wrong bit budget, in an order no codec was designed for. I ran the experiment instead of repeating the advice. The setup, so you can break it A 540×810 frame stands in for "the source you were given" (the demo material downscaled with Lanczos, which is what a capture pipeline hands you); the 1080×1620 original is ground truth. Every path is scored against that with PSNR and SSIM from ffmpeg, plus a blockiness index defined below. No neural upscaler is involved, because the question is codec order, not which model is best — including a model would confound the two. Paths: source straight to 2× Lanczos (oracle); H.264 at bitrate B, decode, then upscale; the same wrapped in FFV1 lossless first (the "transcode to ProRes" advice, tested literally); two lossy encodes then upscale; and upscale first, encode the big frame. Result 1: the lossless transcode changes literally nothing At 700 kbps, encode-then-upscale scored PSNR 32.590, SSIM 0.94663 . Inserting a full FFV1 round trip between decode and upscale produced PSNR 32.590, SSIM 0.94663 . Identical to three decimals, at 300k, 700k and 1500k. Identical because that is what lossless means: decode(H.264) and decode(FFV1(encode(H.264))) are the same pixel array. The transcode either reproduces the decoded frame exactly — you added a step and changed nothing — or it does not, and you added a generation. There is no third outcome. When a tutorial says transcoding "cleans up" artifacts, it is describing a filter doing the work, not a container. Path at 700 kbps PSNR SSIM Blockiness, 16 px grid oracle, no codec 34.202 0.98180 1.083 encode → upscale 32.590 0.94663 1.179 encode → lossless → upscale 32.590 0.94663 1.179 encode → encode again → upscale 32.400 0.94182 1.182 upscale → encode, same 700k 30.623 0.92303 1.363 The last row is why this article exists. Result 2: at equal bits-per-pixel, compressing after the upscale wins That last row looks terrible. The comparison is dishonest, and it is the mistake almost everyone makes. 700 kbps on a 437,400-pixel frame is 1.600 bits per pixel ; the same 700 kbps on the 1,749,600-pixel upscaled frame is 0.400 — a quarter of the budget per pixel. Of course it loses. You asked a codec to describe four times as many pixels with the same bits. Give the big frame four times the bitrate and the ordering reverses: Strategy Bits per pixel PSNR SSIM 700k small → upscale 1.600 32.59 0.9466 upscale → 2800k big 1.600 33.41 0.9673 300k small → upscale 0.686 30.77 0.9160 upscale → 1200k big 0.686 32.12 0.9473 1500k small → upscale 3.429 33.29 0.9601 upscale → 6000k big 3.429 33.88 0.9749 At matched bits-per-pixel, encoding after the resize wins at every rung, by 0.6–1.4 dB. The mechanism is not mysterious. Encoding the small frame spends budget reproducing codec-shaped detail — the DCT basis functions that best approximate the texture — and then the upscaler reconciles those 8×8 patches with its own smoothness prior, amplifying what the codec got wrong, because a resize preserves high-frequency error. Encoding the big frame spends the same budget on the high-frequency content the upscaler actually produced, with no later step to amplify mistakes. In one sentence: pre-encoding pays for compression twice and lets the more artifact-prone pass be the one the upscaler magnifies. Result 3: the block grid does not vanish when you upscale — it moves A codec leaves a discontinuity on an 8-pixel grid, the transform size. Scale by f and the grid lands at period 8*f*. I measured differential gradient energy exactly on the expected period, normalised against off-period energy: 1.0 means no seam, above 1.0 means a periodic seam exists there. Factor Output Expected grid Index at expected period Index at period 8 1.0× 540×810 8 px 1.159 1.159 1.5× 810×1215 12 px 1.237 1.037 2.0× 1080×1620 16 px 1.260 1.195 3.0× 1620×2430 24 px 1.279 1.067 4.0× 2160×3240 32 px 1.293 1.176 The seam energy is still there after 4× — slightly stronger, not weaker, because the resize stretches each seam over more pixels and raises contrast across it. It has simply relocated to period 32. Every deblocker in every editor assumes an 8-pixel grid and will find nothing there, leaving the real artifact untouched. I checked. Deblocking the compressed small frame before the upscale dropped the index 1.260 → 1.117 and cost 0.03 dB. Deblocking after , at the wrong period, dropped it to 0.974 but smeared recovered detail — PSNR flat at 30.78, SSIM +0.0003. Neither is a win. The fix is to not create the grid: encode once, at the end, with enough bits. Result 4: 4:2:0 chroma is gone and upscaling will not bring it back Against a 4:4:4 encode at 1500 kbps, mean absolute Cb/Cr error was 1.108 levels at source resolution, 1.122 after a 2× upscale, and 1.122 after upscaling and re-subsampling. Interpolation cannot invent bandwidth that subsampling destroyed. This is the one part of "transcode first" that is genuinely right — but the reason is chroma headroom, not artifact removal. An intermediate in 4:2:0 caps final colour detail no matter what the last encode gets. Result 5: for stills, a second save is nearly free — pre-sharpening is not Re-saving a JPEG at fixed quality, scored against the original: at q≈70, 41.32 dB for generation one, 41.30 for two, 41.30 for three. At q≈85, 43.41 → 43.40 → 43.40. At q≈92, 44.66 → 44.66 → 44.66. The second generation costs about 0.02 dB, because quantisation is deterministic: the first save already rounded every coefficient to the grid, and saving again lands on the same grid. Generational loss is real but front-loaded. Re-saving at higher quality recovers nothing — 42.217 → 42.183 dB, SSIM unchanged to four decimals; a finer quantiser cannot un-round a coefficient. Pre-sharpening before the lossy save is where people lose money: sharpen then save gave 36.92 dB / 0.9791 , versus 42.22 dB / 0.9839 without. Five dB worse, because sharpening adds high-frequency energy the codec must spend bits on or discard, and discarding it rings exactly where the sharpen halo already is. Sharpen after the last lossy step — with one exception: sharpening before a generative upscaler changes what the model thinks the source distribution is, which is a different question with no general answer. The decision table Situation Pre-encode? What to actually do One H.264 copy → upscale No Decode, upscale, encode once at the end Need an editing intermediate Yes, lossless/RGB ProRes 422 HQ or FFV1 — for chroma and repeated saves, not artifact removal Source is 4:2:0, colour matters Already too late Cannot be restored; capture 4:2:2/4:4:4 next time Artifacts already visible No A denoise/deblock pass is a filter — measure it, don't call it a transcode Platform re-encodes the upload anyway No Encode once at high quality; their pass is your last generation Stills, two or three saves No Loss is front-loaded in save one Stills needing sharpening No Sharpen after the final lossy step Bitrate budget fixed per output No, and this is the trap A fixed total bitrate on a 4× frame is ¼ the bits/px That last row costs people the most. "We have a 10 Mbps budget" is a statement about a delivery target, not a pixel count. Change the pixel count 4× and you silently changed quality 4×. Comparing orderings at equal total bitrate and concluding "compressing after upscale is bad" is measuring your own budget error. When you should not follow any of this When the source is already multi-generation. After three encodes the artifacts are no longer on a clean 8×8 grid; they are smeared across scales and no ordering argument applies. The damage is upstream of every choice here. When the upscaler is generative and expects a specific input distribution. Some models were trained on mildly compressed web images; feeding them pristine lossless frames can push them off-distribution and produce worse output. That inverts the advice — but it is a property of one model, so verify per model rather than generalising. When the intermediate is doing real work. Deinterlacing, denoising, deflickering, colour management are filters. They belong in the pipeline and should be measured on the final output. My result is about the transcode step, not preprocessing in general. When you cannot measure. Everything here is PSNR and SSIM against synthetic ground truth, which rewards fidelity and correlates poorly with perceived quality on generative output. If you cannot look at the result at 100%, do not let a metric decide for you. The two-minute version Encode once, at the end, at a bitrate chosen for the output pixel count rather than inherited from the input. Insert a lossless intermediate only for chroma headroom or repeated edit cycles. Never insert a lossy intermediate to clean up a lossy source. And whenever you compare two orderings, normalise to bits per pixel first — the most common error in this discussion is comparing a well-funded small encode against a starved large one. The preset set and pipeline order I use are documented here

title: Opdo closes $2.3M pre-seed for AI optical engineering
author: Mikhail Savchenko
summary: Opdo, which describes its business as optical engineering built natively around artificial intelligence, has secured $2.3 million in pre-seed financing, Tech. eu reports . The startup operates from Los Angeles and Berlin. Angular Ventures led the round, with Inflection and Tiny.vc taking part. What Opdo builds The company is developing a self-improving system that joins AI-driven design and simulation with data from real manufacturing. Its stated goal is to automate optical engineering from the first design through to finished components. The firm says it has already cut development and production timelines for end-to-end builds from months down to weeks. Over the past year and more, Opdo has partnered with clients on intricate optical systems, combining AI agents with expert engineers. Its technology runs inside established optical design software, including Zemax and CODE V, so engineers keep their current tools. Customers can also source prototypes and finished components through the company. Projects so far cover laser and imaging systems, micro-optics and nanostructured surfaces. The feedback loop The core idea is that data from manufactured and tested components flows back into the AI models. Each later design benefits from what earlier parts showed in production, which Opdo says moves the process step by step toward production-ready systems built from initial requirements. The company points to optics demand in quantum computing, aerospace, AR/VR, defence and advanced sensing, and to a shortage of specialist engineers as the bottleneck. Who is behind it Opdo was founded by Stephan Kuehr (CEO) and Yousef Arzhangnia (CTO). Kuehr previously co-founded 3YOURMIND, a software company that automates distributed manufacturing. The new money is earmarked for expanding the engineering team, developing the AI tooling and taking on more customer projects. Companies with an optical design project can submit a use case on the Opdo website. What is and is not confirmed The months-to-weeks figure comes from the company and its founders; the source gives no customer names, benchmarks or methodology for it. This is an early-stage raise, and the product is currently delivered with Opdo's own engineers involved, not as a self-serve tool.

title: The MCP ecosystem's missing layer is the gateway
author: alanwang100
summary: The Model Context Protocol solved a genuinely hard problem: how an agent describes and invokes tools in a uniform way. Every major agent — Claude, Cursor, Cline, Codex — now speaks MCP, and the protocol has won. But look at how the ecosystem is growing, and there's a pattern worth noticing. The default way to connect an agent to a real system is to write an MCP server. There are thousands of them now — one per API, one per SaaS product, one per internal service. That's fine when you're a SaaS vendor with the engineering capacity to build and maintain a server, plus a registry listing, docs, and an auth story. But most of the systems agents actually need to reach are not MCP servers. They're plain HTTP APIs: internal tools, partner APIs, legacy services, homegrown microservices. For those, "write an MCP server" is the wrong answer. You're not building a product around the tool — you just want the agent to be able to call it. The gateway layer What's missing is a layer between an arbitrary HTTP API and an agent's tool set: a gateway that maps HTTP endpoints to MCP tools without you hand-writing a server. The properties that matter: Declarative, not code. You describe the endpoint; the gateway generates tools/list and handles tools/call . No per-API server to build or maintain. One endpoint, N tools. An agent shouldn't need ten MCP server URLs to use ten services. A gateway aggregates them behind a single streamable-HTTP endpoint — the client configures one URL and gets the whole tool surface. Auth at one choke point. Downstream systems keep their own auth; the gateway holds the credentials and does the exchange, so the agent never sees a raw API key. This is the same story the API-gateway layer already told in the REST world — Kong, Apigee, Envoy — just replayed one level up for agents. Why it matters now Two things are converging. First, the number of agent clients keeps growing, each with its own way of registering MCP servers, which makes "configure once, distribute everywhere" more valuable, not less. Second, agents are starting to call other agents' tools — and when they do, someone has to mediate that traffic: identity, metering, and eventually payment. That's the machine-economy bet: the gateway is where agent-to-agent tool calls get brokered. Where we landed We built this as JiZhiMCP — an agent-first MCP gateway that hosts any HTTP API as MCP tools behind one streamable-HTTP endpoint. One endpoint, N services, auth handled once upstream. It's live on the official MCP Registry (installable from any agent client that reads it) and open on GitHub: https://github.com/alanwang100/jizhineng-mcp The gateway layer is the part of the MCP stack that's still up for grabs. Curious what other people building in this space are seeing — are you still writing servers by hand, or has the gateway pattern started showing up in your stack?

title: Claude Sonnet 4.5 retires on 30 November: find it in your code
author: Karthik Upadrasta
summary: Anthropic retires Claude Sonnet 4.5 ( claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 ) on 30 November 2026 . After that, requests to that model ID on Anthropic's API fail. Anthropic recommends Claude Sonnet 5.5 as the replacement ( Anthropic's notice ). The ID rarely sits in one place. Check: application code and SDK calls .env.example and other environment defaults Terraform variables and Helm values notebooks and eval scripts fallback paths that only run when something else fails The free way rg -n "claude-sonnet-4-5" --hidden -g '!node_modules' It misses IDs built from parts ( f"claude-sonnet-{ver}" ) and aliases, so read the hits around your config loaders too. On Bedrock or Google Cloud? Those platforms set their own retirement dates, which can differ from Anthropic's. Check your platform's page. The automatic way We built SunsetLint , a GitHub App that runs this check against 59 retirement rules (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini), each taken from the provider's own notice. It opens one issue per repo with file, line, date and replacement, and it's read-only. Here's what it posts on our demo repo: issue #1 . Free for public repos and 3 private repos.
